justification: Ran `node tools/run-code.mjs src/content/articles/databases/normalization.md` from PowerShell three times in a row: PASS, blocks=54, executed=30, every time, no flakiness, matching the writer's claim exactly. `node:sqlite` on this machine reports 3.50.4, matching the article's stated '3.50'. I traced every anomaly by hand against the seven-row dataset: the update anomaly really does leave `order_flat` with two different emails for customer 1 across the three shown rows (1001/1001/1004) after the single-row UPDATE, exactly as printed; the insertion anomaly really throws `NOT NULL constraint failed: order_flat.order_id` (order_id is the first NOT NULL column with no value supplied, which is why SQLite names it); the deletion anomaly really leaves zero rows for customer 4 after deleting her only line item, erasing her name and email with nothing else in the table to preserve them. I re-derived the FD closures myself: {order_id, product_id} is the only candidate key of order_flat given the stated rules, and 2NF's partial-dependency list (6 columns depending on order_id alone or product_id alone, only quantity and salesperson_id needing both) is correct. I independently verified the BCNF-specific claims by hand against the actual seven line items: after the 2NF+3NF split, joining order_line/orders/products and grouping by (customer_id, product_category) gives one salesperson per group in all six groups (matches the article's output); the demonstrated UPDATE (order 1004/102 salesperson 1->2) really does make Priya's Fiction group show 2 distinct reps, and the article's own HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT salesperson_id) > 1 query really catches it while every declared constraint (composite PK, NOT NULL) stays satisfied — this is a real, undetected corruption, not a described one. I rebuilt `rep_of`'s six DISTINCT rows by hand from the seven line items (two collapse to one for (1, Fiction, 1)) and confirmed both `GROUP BY customer_id, product_category HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` and `GROUP BY customer_id, salesperson_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 1` are genuinely empty on this data, and that salesperson_id -> product_category genuinely holds (each of the three reps maps to exactly one category) — so {customer_id, product_category} and {customer_id, salesperson_id} are both real, overlapping candidate keys, not asserted ones. I downloaded and text-extracted both cited slide decks directly (pdftotext) rather than trusting citation text: Silberschatz ch.7 defines FD as 't1[a]=t2[a] => t1[b]=t2[b] for any legal relation' (article's paraphrase is accurate and not copied) and 1NF as 'domains of all attributes of R are atomic' / 'domain is atomic if its elements are indivisible units' (again accurately paraphrased, not copied). Critically, I grepped the full extracted text of both decks for 'second normal form' and '2NF' and found zero matches in either — Silberschatz's ch.7 jumps from FD definitions straight to BCNF then 3NF then back to 1NF, and the R&G Ch19_FDs deck covers only FDs/BCNF/3NF. The writer's implicit choice not to cite either source for the 2NF definition is correct: there is no dedicated 2NF slide in either deck to cite. I also confirmed from the same extraction that Silberschatz's `dept_advisor(s_ID, i_ID, dept_name)` example, with FDs `i_ID -> dept_name` and `s_ID, dept_name -> i_ID` and candidate keys `{s_ID, dept_name}`/`{s_ID, i_ID}`, is structurally identical to `rep_of(customer_id, product_category, salesperson_id)` with `salesperson_id -> product_category` and `customer_id, product_category -> salesperson_id` and candidate keys `{customer_id, product_category}`/`{customer_id, salesperson_id}` — a genuine match to the classic textbook pattern, built from the article's own bookstore data rather than copied. I verified the SQLite claims against the live docs: STRICT tables require 3.37.0+ (article says '3.37 or later', correct); an INTEGER column really would store '02138' as 2138 per the Datatypes page (article's claim is correct); `ALTER TABLE ... DROP COLUMN` really does succeed on order_line.salesperson_id since it is not part of a PK, UNIQUE, index, CHECK, FK, generated-column, trigger or view reference (confirmed live by the passing run). The seven-table final decomposition is correct: every table's only determinant is a candidate key or the whole key (orders/customers/zip_codes/products/salespeople trivially by single-column PK, order_line and customer_rep because no FD exists among their remaining columns beyond the composite key), so all seven are genuinely in BCNF with no anomaly path remaining. I compared this against two real published treatments of the same query ('database normalization'): Wikipedia's Database normalization article and GeeksforGeeks's Normal Forms in DBMS page. Both describe every anomaly and normal form in prose over small static example tables; neither runs SQL, and neither has a worked BCNF-vs-3NF example with two overlapping candidate keys (GeeksforGeeks's own BCNF section is generic superkey prose with no such construction; Wikipedia's normal-form comparison is a checklist table). The article's 'every anomaly is real, running SQL' framing and its from-scratch dept_advisor-pattern BCNF example are genuinely differentiated from both. I found no factual error, so the brief's 7.0 cap does not apply. What keeps this below 9.5: (1) the ALTER TABLE paragraph lists four DROP COLUMN restrictions (PK, UNIQUE, index, foreign key) as though that were the complete rule, when SQLite's own docs list four more (partial-index WHERE reference, CHECK constraint, generated-column expression, trigger/view reference) — none apply here so the specific claim about order_line is correct, but a strong student reading only this page would come away with an incomplete picture of the real restriction; (2) the 2NF definition sentence carries no inline citation at all (defensible, since I confirmed neither cited source has one, but the brief's hard rule 3 wants a source for every non-obvious claim and a sentence noting 'neither cited textbook has a dedicated 2NF slide; this follows directly from the FD/candidate-key vocabulary above' would close the gap instead of leaving it implicit); (3) 'Codd's original description of the relational model required exactly this' attributes 1NF's atomicity requirement to Codd by name with no citation to Codd's paper (uncontroversial and consistent with the cited Silberschatz definition, but not itself sourced). All three are sentence-level, none touches the correctness of the SQL, the FD reasoning, or the BCNF derivation.

issues.location: Section 'Boyce-Codd normal form (BCNF) is the fix', paragraph beginning 'order_line.salesperson_id is now redundant': 'SQLite's ALTER TABLE refuses to drop a column that is part of a primary key, a UNIQUE constraint, an index, or a foreign key'
issues.problem: Incomplete as a general statement of SQLite's DROP COLUMN restrictions. The real list (sqlite.org/lang_altertable.html) also refuses a column named in the WHERE clause of a partial index, in a table/column CHECK constraint, in a generated-column expression, or referenced by a trigger or view. None of these apply to order_line.salesperson_id, so the specific claim in the article is still correct, but the sentence reads as if it were the whole rule.
issues.fixLooksLike: Add 'among other conditions' or a parenthetical naming one more (e.g., 'or referenced by a CHECK constraint or a trigger') so the sentence does not imply the list of four is exhaustive.

issues.location: Section 'Second normal form: nothing may depend on half the key', definition sentence: '**second normal form (2NF)** forbids it: every non-key column must depend on the whole key, not a piece of it'
issues.problem: No inline citation. I confirmed by text-extracting both cited slide decks (Silberschatz ch.7 and the Ramakrishnan/Gehrke Ch19_FDs deck) that neither has a dedicated 2NF slide or definition — so the omission is defensible, but the brief's hard rule 3 ('every non-obvious factual claim has a primary source... cite inline where the claim is made') is still not literally satisfied, and a reader has no way to know the gap is deliberate rather than an oversight.
issues.fixLooksLike: One clause noting the gap explicitly, e.g. 'neither of this page's two textbook sources gives 2NF its own definition slide, so this follows directly from the functional-dependency and candidate-key vocabulary already established above.'

issues.location: First section, caption text: 'Codd's original description of the relational model required exactly this'
issues.problem: Attributes the atomicity requirement to Codd by name with no citation to Codd's 1970 paper or any source that discusses it directly. It is a well-known, uncontroversial fact (and consistent with the cited Silberschatz 1NF definition), but as written it is an unsourced historical attribution.
issues.fixLooksLike: Either drop the named attribution to Codd (say 'the relational model's original requirement' without the citation-shaped phrasing) or add a citation for the claim.
